title: Frontiers: Impact of Stay-at-Home-Orders and Cost-of-Living on Stimulus Response: Evidence from the CARES Act
authors: Kanishka Misra; Vishal Singh; Qianyun (Poppy) Zhang
publication: Marketing Science 41(2), 211-229 (2022); Articles in Advance January 19, 2022
screened_from: published_article_text_only (package unusable: archive belongs to another paper)
rescreened_nov4: Earlier record was unassessable: the package under package_dir is another paper's MVAE brand-logo archive and no article text was available. Re-screened from the published article text (data/text/mksc/mksc.2021.1329.txt) and the rendered Figure 7. The fresh INFORMS download of Nov 4 (_incoming/mksc.2021.1329.zip) is byte-identical to the wrong archive (MD5 91c0fa048f0db1a4c52a2b6012f283ec), so the package is still unusable.
eligible_reason: Eligible only through the main-text Nielsen re-analysis (Section 4.3.2, Figure 7 bottom row). The authors re-estimate model 1 of Broda and Parker (2014) on the 2008 Nielsen Consumer Panel and its tax-rebate survey, with household and week fixed effects (figure note: 'based on subsamples ... Nielsen(HH & week) fe'). They print the 4-week dollar impact of receiving the 2008 Economic Stimulus Payment, with SEs, for ten subsamples: ZIP population below median, 50th-90th percentile and top decile, and MSA RPP below and above median, each split by liquidity constraint. The reported effects are dollars per household (8 to 100), not per-dollar propensities, so the regressor is the receipt indicator. Receipt weeks are staggered across households by the IRS disbursement schedule, which gives many weekly adoption cohorts. Each subsample regression is therefore an unstacked TWFE event study of a binary treatment. The article does not restate the equation, bins, controls, weights or clustering, so this rests on Broda and Parker's model 1 and must be verified. The paper's own CARES Act design does not qualify. Eq. (1) regresses daily scaled zip-code spending on leads and lags (j = -1 to 4) of the scaled dollar amount of federal deposits, a continuous and recurring regressor, with zip and county-day FE. This covers Figure 4 (OLS, IV, rebate-only sample, longer panel, PPP falsification), Figure 5, Figure 6 bottom row and Figure A.1; Figure 6 top row is a neural-network two-stage model. The CEX re-analyses in the Figure 7 top row re-estimate the Johnson et al. (2006) and Parker et al. (2013) first-difference regressions on rebate amounts, which have no household FE and a continuous treatment.
design_notes: Main data: Facteus zip-code-by-day debit-card spending and federal deposits (about 12 million cards, 21,570 zip codes in a balanced panel, January 1 to April 17, 2020; a 14,776-zip extension to May 31), plus Census/ACS, Zillow, IRS, Google workplace mobility and BEA RPP. CARES deposits cluster on April 10, 13 and 15, 2020; identification comes from deposit timing across zip codes within county (county-day FE), and the sum of the daily coefficients is the MPC (0.51 overall, 0.29 excluding banking). Footnote 14 cites Goodman-Bacon and argues that the bias does not apply because treatment falls in a short window. Robustness reanalyses: CEX (2001 and 2008 rebates; merged Misra and Surico 2014 replication data with BLS_URBN and POPSIZE) and the Nielsen 2008 rebate survey and household panel (Kilts Center), with ZIP population from the Census and MSA RPP added.
estimators_reported: distributed-lag OLS of daily zip spending on continuous scaled stimulus dollars (leads/lags -1 to 4) with zip and county-day FE (Figures 4-6, A.1)
IV version with the number of deposits instrumenting rebate dollars (Figure 4)
neural-network heterogeneous-effects model with second-stage OLS (Figure 6 top row)
CEX first-difference rebate regressions re-estimated by subsample (Figure 7 top row)
TWFE event study of 2008 rebate receipt with household and week FE, by subsample (Figure 7 bottom row; eligible)
main_or_robustness: robustness (the qualifying specifications are the Nielsen 2008 re-analysis in Section 4.3.2; the main CARES Act design has a continuous, recurring treatment and does not qualify)
n_adoption_cohorts_note: Many weekly receipt cohorts (2008 payments were disbursed from late April to mid-July 2008 by the last two digits of the SSN; paper checks later). The exact number in the re-estimation sample is not reported in this article.
never_treated_note: Unknown; Broda and Parker's sample may consist only of recipient households, in which case comparisons are with not-yet-treated households only.

data_access: proprietary (the qualifying Nielsen specifications use the licensed Nielsen Consumer Panel and its 2008 tax-rebate survey from the Kilts Center; the CARES analyses use Facteus debit-card data that the acknowledgments say are accessible for academic use via the SafeGraph COVID-19 Data Consortium; CEX data are public)
data_files_note: INFORMS archive for this DOI holds another paper's files (verified twice, Nov 1 and Nov 4). Both downloads are byte-identical (MD5 91c0fa048f0db1a4c52a2b6012f283ec): the MVAE brand-logo replication package of another Marketing Science paper (4,674 entries; no CARES, stimulus, stay-at-home, Nielsen or Facteus files), although the article says 'The data file and e-companion are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2021.1329'. Screened from the article only. Nielsen data from Kilts are normally not redistributable, so the qualifying specifications will most likely need Kilts access and the authors' code. The Facteus panel is itself a noise-injected version of bank transaction records (Appendix B quotes Facteus' description of its 'Synthetic Data panel'); this concerns only the ineligible CARES specifications.
software_notes: Unknown: the correct package has not been obtained.
priority_note: Eligible design (Figure 7 Nielsen panels), but no usable package and the data are licensed Nielsen data; needs the authors' code or a rebuild from Kilts data following Broda and Parker (2014).
verification_needed: Confirm against Broda and Parker (2014, J. Monetary Econ. 68:S20-S36), Section 3, and the authors' code: (1) model 1 is a household-and-week FE regression on receipt-week indicators with no other controls; (2) the liquidity split is a separate subsample regression and not a treatment-by-liquidity interaction; (3) bins, leads, weights and clustering. If (2) fails, the ten columns are subgroup-by-treatment interactions and the paper becomes a near-miss; if (1) fails, it is not a staggered binary design.
screener_notes: Screened from the published article (19 pages read in full) and a rendering of Figure 7 at 110 dpi to read the printed estimates; the ten bars are 15(6) and 50(8) below median, 16(5) and 60(7) at the 50th-90th percentile, 13(8) and 100(14) in the top decile, 17(6) and 47(10) for RPP below median, and 8(6) and 80(9) for RPP above median (not constrained, then constrained). The design reading relies on the figure note and on Broda and Parker (2014), which was not available locally and was not downloaded; to my knowledge Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024) use the same Nielsen 2008 rebate design as their empirical application, which supports the reading. The main CARES design would be excluded in any case, as a continuous dose with recurring deposits.
